**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** Recommendation on our inference capacity decision
**Status:** For discussion at Thursday's planning session

Over the past month we've been circling a question that keeps coming back to the same fork in the road: our local inference hardware is running hot during peak hours, queue times are creeping up, and we need to decide whether to purchase additional GPUs or invest in squeezing more out of the fleet we already own. I want to lay out my thinking here so we can debate the substance rather than re-litigate the framing every week.

Let me start with the case that's easiest to quantify. Our current utilisation sits around 70% averaged across the day, but that number hides an ugly peak-to-trough spread. Between 10am and 3pm we're effectively saturated, and p95 latency for interactive requests has drifted from 400ms to nearly 1.2 seconds over the last quarter. Batch workloads absorb the slack overnight, so the pain is concentrated exactly where our users feel it most. Buying two more accelerators would cost roughly £60k upfront plus perhaps £4k annually in power, cooling, and maintenance — a real but manageable hit to our budget, and one that would immediately restore headroom.

The alternative — improving utilisation — is cheaper in cash terms but not free. The promising levers are better request batching, dynamic quantisation for less latency-sensitive traffic, a smarter scheduling layer that preempts batch jobs when interactive demand spikes, and caching of frequent completions. Our own experiments suggest we could lift effective capacity by 25–35% for an engineering cost of maybe six to eight weeks of one engineer's time. That's the number that should give us pause, because it's not really £0 — it's six to eight weeks during which that engineer isn't building the retrieval pipeline or the evaluation harness, both of which are on the critical path for our roadmap. Opportunity cost is the quiet line item in this debate, and I don't want us to pretend it isn't there.

On reliability, the picture cuts both ways. More hardware gives us redundancy: right now a single accelerator failure during peak hours degrades service noticeably, and our failover story is thin. A larger fleet means we can survive a node loss without users noticing. Better utilisation, by contrast, tends to push systems closer to their limits, and tightly optimised schedulers fail in less graceful ways — a bug in preemption logic at 95% load is a worse failure mode than a queue at 60% load. If reliability is our primary concern, buying hardware is the blunter, more forgiving instrument.

Latency is where utilisation work genuinely shines, though. Batching and caching improvements don't just add capacity; they reduce tail latency directly, and some of our scheduling ideas would let us serve interactive traffic with lower p99 than we've ever achieved, even at current load. Hardware alone doesn't buy that — it just moves the saturation point out by a quarter or two, after which we're having this same conversation again.

Then there's reversibility, which I think is the most underweighted factor. Software improvements are highly reversible: if a scheduling change misbehaves, we roll it back in an afternoon. Hardware is not. Once we've spent £60k on accelerators, that capital is committed, and if our workload mix shifts — say, a model change halves our compute per request, or we move some traffic to a hosted API — we're left holding depreciating silicon. Conversely, if demand keeps compounding the way it has, under-buying now means a more expensive scramble later. The asymmetry isn't trivial in either direction, but the software path lets us learn before we commit.

So here is my recommendation, offered with appropriate humility: invest in utilisation first, with a hard time-box of eight weeks and a pre-agreed trigger. If, at the end of that window, peak-hour p95 latency hasn't returned below 600ms, or if utilisation-adjusted demand is still growing faster than our improvements, we buy the two accelerators without further debate. This sequencing preserves our optionality, defers irreversible spending until we understand our true trajectory, and builds scheduling and caching infrastructure we'll want regardless of fleet size.

The honest uncertainty is that our demand forecast is shaky. If a new internal customer onboards next month, the utilisation work may be a detour we can't afford. I'd rather find that out in eight weeks with better data than spend £60k on a guess today.

Looking forward to the discussion — please push back on the time-box if you think it's too generous or too tight.
